subject: Business Models
title: Cross-Subsidization
description: A fast breakdown of Cross-Subsidization for builders.

hook.text: Banks offer free checking accounts. The real revenue comes from overdraft fees: $30 billion/year.

buildup.text: Cross-subsidization makes one product free (or cheap) and profits from a related paid product.

discovery.text: Google gives away Android free. Revenue comes from Search and Play Store fees on every Android phone.

twist.text: The subsidized product builds dependency. Once you're on Android, Google's ads follow you everywhere.

climax.text: Cross-subsidies hide the true cost. The 'free' thing is always paid for somewhere else.

punchline.text: Free checking, $35 overdraft fees. The subsidy always hides a tax.

quiz.question: How does Google profit from giving away Android?
options: Search ads and Play Store fees

details.summary: Cross-subsidization uses profits from one product or customer segment to subsidize another that drives strategic value. Amazon sells devices at cost to drive Prime subscriptions. Banks offer free checking accounts funded by loan interest. Consoles sell below cost funded by game royalties.
details.whyItMatters: Cross-subsidization allows businesses to compete aggressively on price in one area while earning profits elsewhere. Understanding which side of the business funds which reveals the real strategy behind seemingly irrational pricing decisions.
takeaways: Profits from one product fund below-cost pricing on another
The subsidized product typically drives adoption of the profitable one
Competitors who cannot cross-subsidize face structural disadvantage

faq.question: How does Amazon use cross-subsidization strategically?
faq.answer: Kindle and Echo devices are sold at or below cost to lock users into Amazon's content and commerce ecosystem. Prime membership subsidizes free shipping to drive purchase frequency. AWS profits subsidize aggressive pricing in retail. Each business funds the others' competitive advantages.

faq.question: When does cross-subsidization become anti-competitive?
faq.answer: When a dominant company uses profits from a monopoly market to price below cost in a competitive market, driving out competitors who cannot match the pricing. Regulators investigate this as predatory pricing. Google's free products funded by search advertising face this criticism.
